B2-a: A school picture-day portrait from around 2003, the kind of glossy print that came home in a cardboard folder with a sheet of wallet-sized copies. A figure in a plain black knitted balaclava sits upright on a low photographer's stool, shoulders turned slightly to one side the way pupils were always angled, chin a touch down, the masked face turned dead to the lens with calm, polite stillness. The balaclava has no eye, nose or mouth holes, so no skin shows anywhere; a large white ring is stitched round the whole face, and one small red triangle with rounded corners, pointing down, sits high inside the ring on the right-hand side of the picture. Black woollen gloves rest one over the other on its knee, and it wears a tidy navy V-neck school jumper over a white collared shirt, collar slightly crooked. Behind it hangs the familiar mottled canvas backdrop, cloudy grey-blue darkening toward the edges, softly out of focus. The light is flat and forgiving: a big soft main light from front-left and a gentle fill, so the mask, ring and triangle are evenly lit with almost no shadow, plus a faint hair light rimming the top of the head. Head-and-shoulders crop, centred, medium telephoto compression, camera at chest height. The colour is that slightly too-smooth, warm-skewed minilab print of the era: lifted blacks, creamy highlights, a gentle magenta-blue cast, fine grain and the soft sheen of photo paper. Ordinary, wholesome, and very wrong. The print is clean: no writing, digits, name plates or stamps.
B2-b: A still lifted from somebody's family videotape, late 1990s, a birthday do in a cramped front room filmed by an uncle with a palm-sized tape camcorder. Twisted paper streamers in red, green and yellow droop from the light fitting, a balloon has drifted against the woodchip wallpaper, and a folding table under a plastic party cloth holds sausage rolls on a foil tray, a bowl of crisps, a hedgehog of cheese-and-pineapple sticks stuck in half a grapefruit, a wobbly orange jelly and paper cups. Behind the table the relatives are dancing to something on the stereo, cardigans and loud patterned shirts swinging, their arms and faces dragged into soft combed smears by the motion; a grandad in a paper crown is laughing at the back. Mid shot, the lens wide and slightly bowed at the frame edges. Closest to camera, filling the lower middle of the portrait frame, stands one extra guest in a plain dark-grey knitted ski mask and plain knitted gloves, nothing of them uncovered. The balaclava has no eye, nose or mouth holes, so no skin shows anywhere; a large white ring is stitched round the whole face, and one small red triangle with rounded corners, pointing down, sits high inside the ring on the right-hand side of the picture. One gloved hand holds a sagging paper plate with a single sausage roll on it. They have turned their head to meet the camcorder dead on, perfectly still, polite, patient, as though about to say thank you for having me. Nobody behind them has clocked it. The camcorder's built-in lamp blasts a flat, frontal, shadowless pool of white light onto the masked head and shoulders so the knit texture, the white ring and the red triangle are crisp and evenly lit, while the room behind drops off into warm tungsten amber and muddy brown with a soft dark vignette. Tape-era texture: colours soft and smeared sideways past their edges, a red-orange glow bleeding off the foil and the bright cups, shadows noisy and crawling with grain, blacks milky and lifted, a slight handheld tilt. Warm, daft, happy and homely, with one guest who does not belong. The picture carries no words, digits, date overlay or symbols of any kind.
B2-c: A night photo from a travelling funfair around 2003, snapped on a cheap pocket digital camera with its built-in xenon flash going off at point-blank range, the sort of hasty holiday shot that later turns up in a happy throwback slideshow. Centre of the frame, seen from about the waist up and from slightly beneath, stands a figure in a plain dark-navy knitted ski mask and thick woollen gloves, body square to the lens, the masked face turned straight out with mild, patient politeness. The balaclava has no eye, nose or mouth holes, so no skin shows anywhere; a large white ring is stitched round the whole face, and one small red triangle with rounded corners, pointing down, sits high inside the ring on the right-hand side of the picture. The whole face area is evenly lit, sharp and clear. In one gloved hand it holds a huge cloud of bubblegum-pink candyfloss on a paper stick; from the other hangs a tied clear plastic bag of water with a single orange goldfish won at a hook-a-duck stall. The flash makes the figure bright, flat and a little overexposed, with a hard dark shadow tucked close behind it, while everything further back falls away into night: the waltzer cars and the light-bulb arches of the rides are only long wobbly trails of magenta, lime, gold and electric blue where the slow shutter dragged them during a small hand shake, floating in a deep black sky speckled with coloured digital noise. Over-saturated early sensor colour, a cool blue tint on the flash-lit wool, purple fringing around the brightest lamps, mild softness at the edges, frame leaning a few degrees. Canopies and booths are plain blank fabric, and nothing in the image carries letters, numbers, signs or symbols. Thanks.
